title: Field norm on a finite domain algebra over a normal domain and contraction of primes
statement: Let $B\hookrightarrow A$ be an inclusion of commutative integral domains, meaning nonzero commutative rings without zero divisors, with $A$ a finite $B$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Let $L\hookrightarrow K$ be a finite-dimensional field extension [def-pc-field-extension], with embeddings $B\hookrightarrow L$ and $A\hookrightarrow K$ whose square commutes and makes $L$ a field of fractions of $B$ and $K$ a field of fractions of $A$ (every field element is a quotient of images with nonzero denominator). Suppose $B$ is integrally closed in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Put $d=\dim_LK\geq1$ [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], and define $N_{K/L}(x)=\det_L(z\mapsto xz\mid K)$ [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant]. There is a unique map $n:A\to B$ whose image in $L$ is $N_{K/L}(a)$ for each $a\in A$; it preserves multiplication and $1$, and $n(b)=b^d$ for $b\in B$. For every $a\in A$ there is a monic $Q_a(T)\in B[T]$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring] with $Q_a(a)=0$ whose coefficientwise image in $L[T]$ is the monic polynomial of least degree annihilating $a\in K$. If $m=\deg Q_a\geq1$ and $e=\dim_{L(a)}K\geq1$, where $L(a)$ is the smallest subfield of $K$ containing $L$ and $a$, then $n(a)=((-1)^mQ_a(0))^e$. For every prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset A$ and every $a\in\mathfrak q$, one has $n(a)\in\mathfrak q\cap B$. Here prime means a proper ideal such that $xy\in\mathfrak q$ implies $x\in\mathfrak q$ or $y\in\mathfrak q$; contraction uses the specified inclusion. No normality of $A$, Noetherian, flatness or separability hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: Fix $a\in A$. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral], module-finiteness of $A$ over $B$ implies that $a$ is integral over $B$. Apply [lem-sfb-integral-minpoly-fraction-descent] to $B\hookrightarrow A$: the base $B$ is integrally closed and both rings are domains. It gives a monic $Q_a\in B[T]$ with $Q_a(a)=0$ whose image is the minimal polynomial $P_a$ over $L$. The specified fraction fields are the fraction fields used by that lemma: the identification sends $b/c$ to the quotient of the specified images, and similarly for $A$ and $K$. These identifications commute with the inclusions because the given square commutes; hence the lemma applies to the specified extension, not a different embedding.

Apply [lem-sfb-finite-field-norm-minpoly] to the given finite extension $L\hookrightarrow K$ and the image of $a$. Since coefficientwise inclusion is injective, the monic polynomials $Q_a$ and $P_a$ have the same degree $m$. The cited statement gives $m\geq1$, $e=\dim_{L(a)}K\geq1$, and $N_{K/L}(a)=((-1)^mP_a(0))^e$. Therefore this norm is the image of the element $((-1)^mQ_a(0))^e\in B$. Define $n(a)$ to be that element. As $a$ was arbitrary, this defines $n:A\to B$ with the required comparison and formula. Any other such map agrees pointwise after the injective embedding $B\hookrightarrow L$, so equals $n$.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-finite-field-norm-minpoly], the field norm preserves multiplication and $1$ and takes each scalar $b\in L$ to $b^d$. Thus the images in $L$ of $n(aa')$ and $n(a)n(a')$ coincide, as do those of $n(1)$ and $1$, and those of $n(b)$ and $b^d$ for $b\in B$. Injectivity of $B\hookrightarrow L$ gives each asserted equality in $B$.

source.place: Tag 0BIF (fields-definition-trace-norm), paragraph immediately after the definition; Divisors Tag 0BD3, property (1).

proof.text: Let $a\in\mathfrak q$, put $c_0=Q_a(0)$, and write $Q_a(T)=c_0+T R_a(T)$ with $R_a\in B[T]$ by shifting the positive-degree coefficients. The equality $Q_a(a)=0$ gives $c_0=-aR_a(a)$ in $A$. Closure of the ideal $\mathfrak q$ under multiplication and subtraction implies that the image of $c_0$ belongs to $\mathfrak q$. The formula from step 2 and $e\geq1$ then imply that the image of $n(a)=((-1)^m c_0)^e$ belongs to $\mathfrak q$. Since $n(a)\in B$, it belongs to $\mathfrak q\cap B$ by the definition of contraction. This argument includes $a=0$ and $m=1$, and uses only the ideal axioms; primality is more than is needed.
